metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both expand or split a radical quotient into fractional powers and then apply the power rule term by term; the candidate asks for the formula instead of its value.
sharedKnowledge: Both expand or split a radical quotient into fractional powers and then apply the power rule term by term; the candidate asks for the formula instead of its value.

matches.rationale: Both simplify a radical denominator to powers, differentiate and substitute a specified positive input.
sharedKnowledge: Both simplify a radical denominator to powers, differentiate and substitute a specified positive input.

matches.rationale: Both select the number of reciprocal-factor choices by equating the total power of x to the requested exponent, then compute the binomial coefficient.
sharedKnowledge: Both select the number of reciprocal-factor choices by equating the total power of x to the requested exponent, then compute the binomial coefficient.

matches.rationale: Both track which selections of terms contribute a targeted power. This candidate combines low-degree contributions from a polynomial product, extending coefficient selection rather than repeating the negative-power equation.
sharedKnowledge: Both track which selections of terms contribute a targeted power. This candidate combines low-degree contributions from a polynomial product, extending coefficient selection rather than repeating the negative-power equation.

matches.rationale: Both recover the combined total from unequal weighted contributions. Here mixture volumes weight ingredient percentages, whereas journey durations weight speeds; the candidate does not test a logical counterexample.
sharedKnowledge: Both recover the combined total from unequal weighted contributions. Here mixture volumes weight ingredient percentages, whereas journey durations weight speeds; the candidate does not test a logical counterexample.

matches.rationale: Both retain both cosine signs after an equation involving a square or modulus, reject impossible levels and count intersections on the stated interval; this candidate finally sums the roots.
sharedKnowledge: Both retain both cosine signs after an equation involving a square or modulus, reject impossible levels and count intersections on the stated interval; this candidate finally sums the roots.

matches.rationale: Both split a squared cosine equation into its two levels, rescale the angular interval and count all permitted branches, with endpoint checks.
sharedKnowledge: Both split a squared cosine equation into its two levels, rescale the angular interval and count all permitted branches, with endpoint checks.

matches.rationale: Both construct an allowed quadrilateral satisfying the stated side or diagonal conditions while violating an unjustified stronger shape property; the candidate distinguishes necessity from sufficiency.
sharedKnowledge: Both construct an allowed quadrilateral satisfying the stated side or diagonal conditions while violating an unjustified stronger shape property; the candidate distinguishes necessity from sufficiency.

matches.rationale: Both test whether perpendicular diagonals or related quadrilateral conditions force a square or stronger symmetry, retaining all premises when constructing a nonsquare example.
sharedKnowledge: Both test whether perpendicular diagonals or related quadrilateral conditions force a square or stronger symmetry, retaining all premises when constructing a nonsquare example.

matches.rationale: Both separate function height from derivative information and construct a polynomial counterexample satisfying an all-input monotonicity premise. The candidate additionally distinguishes first from second derivative ordering.
sharedKnowledge: Both separate function height from derivative information and construct a polynomial counterexample satisfying an all-input monotonicity premise. The candidate additionally distinguishes first from second derivative ordering.

matches.rationale: Both audit an algebraic solution by substituting candidates into the original radical equation and locating a non-equivalent step. The original loses a root by division; this candidate gains one by squaring.
sharedKnowledge: Both audit an algebraic solution by substituting candidates into the original radical equation and locating a non-equivalent step. The original loses a root by division; this candidate gains one by squaring.

matches.rationale: Both identify the first invalid inference in a displayed argument and verify the earlier steps on their domain. The candidate tests an unjustified product inference instead of a zero-divisor cancellation.

matches.rationale: Both translate reflections and shifts into identities in an arbitrary function and rename the universally quantified input to compare equivalent conditions.

matches.rationale: Both identify the centre of paired inputs in an identity for an arbitrary function. Opposite values around the integration midpoint then give cancellation; this is rotational rather than reflection symmetry.

matches.rationale: Both locate the first step that drops the negative possibility when reversing a square, retaining principal-root and trigonometric sign information.

lessons.title: Factor, cancel and rearrange
knowledge: Factor numerators and denominators before cancelling common factors.
Keep the original excluded denominator values after simplification.
Rearrange by collecting the requested subject; distinguish an identity from an equation.

lessons.title: Solve quadratics and use their roots
knowledge: Solve quadratic equations by factorisation or the quadratic formula, retaining both signs.
Use the sum and product of roots to evaluate symmetric expressions.
Build a quadratic from its roots and check the requested quantity.

lessons.title: Mark boundaries and test intervals
knowledge: Mark numerator zeros and excluded denominator values before testing interval signs.
Intersect simultaneous inequalities and retain the appropriate endpoints.
Interpret an absolute-value distance bound as an interval.
Do not multiply an inequality by an expression whose sign is unknown.

lessons.title: Use index laws and one common base
knowledge: Use positive-base index laws, including negative and fractional exponents.
Convert powers to a common positive base other than 1 before equating exponents.
Replace a repeated exponential by a positive variable and recover the original input with logarithms.

lessons.title: Find the inner range first
knowledge: Replace an inner function by a variable with its exact attainable range.
Optimise a quadratic on that range by checking admissible vertices and endpoints.
Distinguish an unattained boundary from an attained extreme.
Use the sine/cosine range and the reversed ordering of positive reciprocals.

lessons.title: Sum an arithmetic block
knowledge: Identify the exact first term, last term and inclusive number of terms in an arithmetic block.
Use equal averages of symmetric AP terms and arithmetic sum formulae.
Subtract partial sums to isolate a block; logarithms of powers can reveal an AP of exponents.

lessons.title: Expand or select the required coefficient
knowledge: An expanded product selects one summand from each bracket.
For one coefficient, enumerate every selection whose powers add to the target, multiply its numerical factors, then add the contributions.
Use binomial coefficients and factorials to count bracket choices.
Track the exponent contributed by a selected term such as x² and keep negative coefficients inside their powers.

lessons.title: Move the input and the height
knowledge: Find transformed points by equating the new inner expression to the old input, then transform the old height.
Interpret translations, stretches and reflections through their effect on input and output.
A negative output multiplier exchanges maxima and minima; successive transformations follow the stated order.

lessons.title: Read the input scale of a trig graph
knowledge: Work with the whole trigonometric input to find periods, zeros and peaks.
Convert radians and degrees and use exact values for standard angles.
Sine and cosine have period 2π and range [−1,1]; tangent has period π and asymptotes π/2+kπ.
Use even cosine and odd sine/tangent symmetry; tangent as sine divided by cosine requires nonzero cosine.

lessons.title: Keep the interval and the original signs
knowledge: Transform the interval along with the trigonometric input and retain every branch in that interval.
Use sin²x+cos²x=1 to reduce an equation to one trigonometric function.
Factor instead of dividing away possible zero factors.
Check original signs after squaring; sqrt(a²)=|a| and denominator exclusions still apply.

lessons.title: Choose a rule and retain both triangles
knowledge: Choose sine or cosine rule according to the known sides and angles.
Retain both valid triangles in an SSA situation and reject degenerate or incompatible candidates.
Use the included angle in the triangle-area formula.
Identify the relevant plane before applying triangle rules in three dimensions.

lessons.title: Rewrite powers before differentiating
knowledge: Rewrite quotients, roots and products as sums of powers before differentiating.
Apply the power rule to rational exponents on the appropriate domain.
Differentiate twice before evaluating a requested second derivative.

lessons.title: Read the shape from derivative signs
knowledge: Factor the derivative and test its sign between zeros and domain breaks.
Use derivative sign changes to classify local maxima and minima.
A zero derivative without a sign change need not be a local extreme.
Use the original function to find stationary-point heights.

lessons.title: Separate signed accumulation from total area
knowledge: Distinguish a signed integral from total geometric area.
Find all intersections and integrate upper minus lower on each separate region.
Split when a curve crosses or an absolute-value formula changes.
The worked absolute-value example treats negative and nonnegative inputs separately.

lessons.title: Turn a ratio into an equation
knowledge: Convert a ratio of quantities into an equation before solving.
Name a repeated exponential as a positive variable to obtain a quadratic.
Reject nonpositive values of the substituted exponential and use its monotonicity to select the largest input.

The combination factor counts which brackets supply bx; powers retain all numerical factors.
Count coefficients by their indices and check end cases separately.
Assess divisibility using prime factors from both the powers and the combination factor.

Transform the whole input interval and count endpoint solutions carefully.
State the tangent domain and multiply by a denominator only within that domain.
Factor rather than divide by a possibly zero factor, list each branch, and remove duplicate solutions.

Evaluate turning heights on the original function to count axis crossings or intersections with a horizontal level.

Check the positive half of the graph and its height at zero when counting positive roots.

Translate mixture percentages into ingredient amounts.

lessons.title: Simplify surds and rationalise

Multiply by a nonzero conjugate to rationalise a denominator.

Keep sqrt(x²)=|x| and all original denominator exclusions.

lessons.title: Circle angles, chords and tangents

Apply centre/circumference, semicircle, same-segment, cyclic-quadrilateral and alternate-segment angle results to the correct chord or arc.
Separate internal and external circle-contact cases using centre distance and radii.
Use a right triangle for an internal common tangent of equal circles.

lessons.title: Turn proportion into a multiplier

Write direct or inverse proportionality using a fixed constant.
Translate ratios into fractions of a whole and use the correct length, area or volume scale.
Distinguish simple interest, compound growth and the order of deposits or withdrawals.

lessons.title: Read tables and histograms

Estimate grouped means using midpoints and distinguish grouped estimates from exact summaries.
Find mean, median, mode and range from frequency data.
Select and construct suitable bar, pie, pictogram, two-way, discrete-line, time-series or cumulative displays.

lessons.title: Estimate an integral with trapezia
knowledge: Use n+1 heights for n trapezium strips and double only the interior heights.
Compute unequal-width trapezia individually.
Determine over- or underestimation from chord position relative to the curve, rather than increasing/decreasing behaviour.
Track signed approximation error through scaling and constants; recognise an exact semicircle integral geometrically.

lessons.title: Read the domain, then AND, OR and NOT
knowledge: Fix the allowed inputs before deciding whether a statement is true.
AND requires both statements; inclusive OR permits either or both; NOT reverses the truth of the whole statement.
Negating a strict inequality includes its equality boundary.
Count whole true statements at the same input when exactly two or exactly one are required.
Some means at least one; not prime is not equivalent to composite because 1 is neither.

lessons.title: Translate IF and ONLY IF before reasoning
knowledge: Identify the premise and conclusion by rewriting a sentence as an if-then implication.
A if B means B implies A; A only if B means A implies B.
If and only if requires both implication directions.
An implication fails precisely when its premise is true and its conclusion false; a false premise is not a counterexample.
A restriction on selected objects need not require any objects to be selected.

lessons.title: Reverse and negate for the contrapositive
knowledge: The converse reverses an implication and needs its own justification.
The contrapositive reverses and negates both clauses and is equivalent to the original implication.
A true premise forces its conclusion, and a false conclusion forces a false premise.
Knowing the conclusion alone does not establish the premise; denying the premise does not deny the conclusion.
Chains of implications can rule out statements as the sole true statement.

lessons.title: Test NECESSARY and SUFFICIENT separately
knowledge: Keep the target fixed: sufficiency tests condition implies target, while necessity tests target implies condition.
Classify a condition by proving each successful direction and giving an allowed counterexample for each failed direction.
Necessary and sufficient describes both directions, as in an if-and-only-if condition.
A stronger condition may be sufficient without being necessary.
For ax+by=c with nonzero coefficients, gradient and intercept signs are determined by -a/b and c/b.

lessons.title: Who is chosen first: EVERY or SOME?
knowledge: Every quantifies over all allowed inputs; there exists requires at least one allowed witness.
Read nested choices in order: a later witness may depend on an earlier input.
One fixed witness working for all inputs is a stronger requirement than choosing a witness separately for each input.
Construct a witness to prove existence and choose a defeating input to disprove a proposed fixed universal witness.
The same existence statement may change truth when its domain changes from integers to reals.

lessons.title: Negate the whole claim, keeping the domain
knowledge: Negate from the outer quantifier inward, swapping every and there exists without changing their order or domains.
The failure of a universal statement is one allowed counterexample; the failure of existence means all allowed candidates fail.
Negating AND gives an OR of negations, while negating OR gives an AND of negations.
To negate an implication, require its premise and the negation of its conclusion.
An if-and-only-if statement fails when exactly one of its two conditions is true; preserve equality when negating inequalities.

lessons.title: Disprove a claim with one allowed example
knowledge: A counterexample must satisfy every hypothesis and violate the conclusion.
For an implication, a true premise and false conclusion are both required.
One counterexample disproves an always-claim, while many successful cases do not prove it.
Check divisibility and primality against their definitions when choosing an integer counterexample.
Negative real inputs can defeat claims that squaring preserves order.

lessons.title: Turn definitions into a direct proof
knowledge: Represent arbitrary even integers as 2k and arbitrary odd integers as 2k+1, with integer k.
Use separate variables for independently chosen integers.
A direct proof begins with the assumptions and uses justified algebra to expose the required form.
To prove divisibility, express the result as the divisor times an integer.
Algebraic representations cover all permitted inputs; numerical tests alone do not.

lessons.title: Cover every case
knowledge: Choose cases that exhaust the stated domain and prove the claim in every case.
Even and odd cases include all integers, including zero and negative integers.
Use |x|=x for x>=0 and |x|=-x for x<0; assign boundary points to a case.
Integer squares leave remainder 0 or 1 modulo 4, as shown by parity cases.
For sums of absolute values, split at each point where an inner expression changes sign.

lessons.title: Assume the opposite and find an impossibility
knowledge: A contradiction proof assumes the denial of the desired conclusion and identifies a precise incompatible fact.
Rationals are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, and division by a nonzero rational.
Use rational closure to prove a rational plus an irrational, or a nonzero rational times an irrational, is irrational.
The impossibility of a negative real square can finish an inequality contradiction.
Showing a numerator and denominator share a factor contradicts rational representation only when lowest terms was assumed.

lessons.title: Find the first unsupported step
knowledge: Check each inference using only the assumptions and earlier justified lines, and stop at the first unsupported step.
A true conclusion does not make an invalid or incomplete proof correct.
Circular reasoning assumes the conclusion that the proof is meant to establish.
Dividing by an expression that may vanish can lose a solution; rearrangement and factorisation retain that case.
Squaring is valid forwards, but its candidate roots must be checked in the original equation.

lessons.title: Check what division loses and squaring adds
knowledge: Before cancelling an expression, check and handle the case where it equals zero.
Rearranging to a zero product can preserve solutions that division would discard.
Squaring an equality gives a necessary condition, but the squared equation may contain additional candidate roots.
Substitute candidates back into the original equation, respecting the nonnegative square root.
Equal function outputs need not imply equal inputs, as with squares and supplementary sine values.

lessons.title: Track signs before using an algebraic rule
knowledge: Multiplication or division by a negative number reverses an inequality.
An unknown multiplier sign may require positive, negative and zero cases.
For c>0, |z|>=c means z<=-c or z>=c, including both equality endpoints.
The zero-product rule requires a product equal to zero; a nonzero product does not fix individual factors.
Use the stated signs to bound ratios of negative numbers.

lessons.title: Separate height, gradient and signed area
knowledge: Function value, derivative and integral represent different quantities and must be tested separately.
Adding a constant changes height without changing the derivative.
A zero derivative gives a horizontal tangent and need not give a maximum or minimum.
Check behaviour on both sides before classifying a stationary point.
A zero signed integral can result from cancellation and does not force zero geometric area or a zero function.

lessons.title: Test both directions with allowed examples
knowledge: Test sufficiency and necessity as separate implications, using allowed counterexamples for directions that fail.
A sorted odd-length list has a middle entry; an even-length median averages the middle two entries.
Repetitions may make an even-length median an entry, while distinctness changes that conclusion.
Do not add assumptions such as positive, distinct or nonzero unless stated.
Apply the direction tests to divisibility, equations, inequalities and logarithmic conditions.

lessons.title: Check the argument, not just the conclusion
knowledge: Locate the first inference not supported by earlier proof lines.
A true one-way implication does not establish its converse; even a true converse needs justification.
A polynomial having no real linear factors does not imply that its integer values are prime.
Squaring gives candidates that require substitution into the original equation.
Cancellation requires a nonzero factor; rational closure can supply the contradiction in irrationality proofs.

lessons.title: Collect all contributions to a coefficient
knowledge: To find a coefficient in a product, list every pair of exponents whose sum is the target exponent.
Multiply the matching coefficients and add all contributions.
The coefficient of x^k in (1+x)^n is the binomial coefficient n choose k.
Substituting x=1 sums all coefficients; it gives one target coefficient only when the contributing terms exhaust that whole row.
For a constant term with positive and negative powers, require the total exponent to be zero.

lessons.title: Use the interval before comparing values
knowledge: Establish an ordering throughout the allowed interval before applying an outer function.
On 0<x<1, x^2<x<sqrt(x).
An exponential base greater than 1 preserves exponent order, while a base between 0 and 1 reverses it.
For continuous functions on [a,b] with a<b, strict pointwise ordering throughout (a,b) gives the same strict ordering of their integrals from a to b.
Read |x-a| as distance from a; midpoint boundaries solve comparisons of distances and intersections of their solution intervals.

lessons.title: Use geometry to test a universal claim
knowledge: Translate a geometric condition into lengths, areas or angles before deciding what it forces.
Triangle area with two sides and the included angle is half the product of the sides and the sine of that angle.
For angles strictly between 0 and 180 degrees, equal sine allows equal or supplementary angles.
A nonsquare rectangle inscribed in a circle gives equal centre-to-side triangle areas without regularity.
A symmetric example proves possibility, while a universal symmetry claim needs proof or an allowed irregular counterexample.

lessons.title: Complete each stage of a proof
knowledge: Existence needs an allowed solution; uniqueness needs proof that every solution equals that candidate.
A necessary candidate condition must be completed by substitution in the original problem or by reversible steps.
A contradiction proof retains the original assumptions, denies the target and finishes with explicitly incompatible facts.
Order definitions and conditions before proof lines that use them.
Rewrite logarithm definitions as powers and regroup exponents to connect a longer chain without assuming its conclusion.
Equal products do not force equality of corresponding factors.

lessons.title: Integer cases and supplied definitions
knowledge: Cover every possible remainder modulo a positive integer to prove a divisibility or remainder claim.
A prime divisible by another prime must equal that prime, so check the prime itself before declaring a multiple composite.
Products of consecutive integers provide small factors; divisibility by 2 and 3 ensures divisibility by 6, but overlapping factors cannot be counted twice.
For a supplied definition, preserve the order of member, factor and partner choices, allowing later choices to depend on earlier ones.
Negating every member has a suitable choice means one member has no suitable choice.
Keep other-member restrictions explicit: self-divisibility cannot supply a different partner.

lessons.title: Use an identity at useful inputs
knowledge: An identity holds at every allowed input; useful substitutions can make function arguments coincide or produce simultaneous equations.
Opposite heights equally spaced around a centre imply a zero value at that centre and signed integral cancellation on intervals with that midpoint.
Symmetry about one centre does not guarantee cancellation on an interval with a different midpoint.
Write the transformed input for each graph operation, then compare the two operation orders.
An identity f(x+T)=f(x) establishes a period, not necessarily the smallest positive period; positive integer multiples are also periods.
Replacing x by -x reflects roots and exchanges their positive and negative signs.

lessons.title: Find the full parameter range
knowledge: Check parameter values at which an equation changes degree before using a quadratic discriminant or dividing by a coefficient.
A nondegenerate quadratic has two distinct real roots for positive discriminant and one distinct repeated root for zero discriminant.
The substitution u=x^2 retains u>=0: positive u gives two real x values, zero gives one and negative u gives none.
Two distinct positive roots of the quadratic in u are needed for four distinct real roots of an even quartic; use discriminant, root sum and product.
Use cubic turning heights to classify real-root counts and inspect zero turning heights at parameter boundaries.
Prove the full necessary-and-sufficient range; a narrower sufficient condition alone does not describe all successful parameters.

lessons.title: Test claims about whole functions
knowledge: A functional counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis everywhere on the required domain or interval.
Increasing function height does not imply increasing gradient, and positive height does not imply positive gradient.
An integral of a square is nonnegative, while an ordinary signed integral may cancel.

On a nonempty forward interval, subtract shared integration intervals to isolate a sign constraint; for a continuous function, a nonpositive integral forces at least one nonpositive value, not nonpositivity everywhere.
The distinct roots of a product are the combined roots of its factors, with overlaps counted once.
A nonzero cubic has opposite-sign tails and cannot be positive on the entire real line.

Keep the original excluded denominator values after simplification.
Rearrange by collecting the requested subject; distinguish an identity from an equation.

knowledge: Factor the derivative and test its sign between zeros and domain breaks.
Use derivative sign changes to classify local maxima and minima.
A zero derivative without a sign change need not be a local extreme.
Use the original function to find stationary-point heights.

lessons.title: Separate signed accumulation from total area
knowledge: Distinguish a signed integral from total geometric area.
Find all intersections and integrate upper minus lower on each separate region.
Split when a curve crosses or an absolute-value formula changes.
The worked absolute-value example treats negative and nonnegative inputs separately.

lessons.title: Turn a ratio into an equation
knowledge: Convert a ratio of quantities into an equation before solving.
Name a repeated exponential as a positive variable to obtain a quadratic.
Reject nonpositive values of the substituted exponential and use its monotonicity to select the largest input.

lessons.title: Keep every factor in a binomial coefficient
knowledge: Use the complete coefficient nCk·a^(n−k)·b^k in (a+bx)^n.
The combination factor counts which brackets supply bx; powers retain all numerical factors.
Count coefficients by their indices and check end cases separately.
Assess divisibility using prime factors from both the powers and the combination factor.

lessons.title: Count solutions without losing a branch
knowledge: Keep separate branches of a trigonometric equation, including both signs when taking a square root.
Transform the whole input interval and count endpoint solutions carefully.
State the tangent domain and multiply by a denominator only within that domain.
Factor rather than divide by a possibly zero factor, list each branch, and remove duplicate solutions.

lessons.title: Use the two possible triangles
knowledge: Use a common triangle height to turn an area ratio into a side ratio.
Model the two possible side lengths as roots of one cosine-rule quadratic.
Compare root sums/products or subtract Pythagoras equations to eliminate a shared height.
For an acute given angle, compare the opposite side with the perpendicular height and adjacent side to count possible SSA triangles.

lessons.title: Count roots from the turning heights
knowledge: Use derivative signs to divide a graph into monotonic pieces.
Evaluate turning heights on the original function to count axis crossings or intersections with a horizontal level.
Count a touching root once and use strict inequalities when distinct roots are required.
Check the positive half of the graph and its height at zero when counting positive roots.

lessons.title: Recover the totals behind the means
knowledge: Recover totals from means and observation counts.
Track conserved combined totals during a swap and changed counts after removal.
Compute pooled means with correct population weights.
Translate mixture percentages into ingredient amounts.

lessons.title: Read the terms before choosing a sum
knowledge: Write initial terms and use the rule to distinguish a geometric progression from a periodic sequence.
A shift of k positions scales an equal-length GP block by r^k.
For an autonomous one-term recurrence u(n+1)=f(u(n)), a repeated value restarts the cycle; a recurrence depending on several terms or on n requires its full state and index phase to repeat.
Count inclusive endpoints, split periodic sums into complete cycles and a remainder, and check infinite-GP convergence.

lessons.title: Simplify surds and rationalise
knowledge: Extract square factors and combine like surds.
Multiply by a nonzero conjugate to rationalise a denominator.
Factor a difference of squares to simplify a surd quotient before calculus.
Keep sqrt(x²)=|x| and all original denominator exclusions.

lessons.title: Circle angles, chords and tangents
knowledge: Add the radius at a tangent or the perpendicular from centre to chord to obtain a right triangle.
Apply centre/circumference, semicircle, same-segment, cyclic-quadrilateral and alternate-segment angle results to the correct chord or arc.
Separate internal and external circle-contact cases using centre distance and radii.
Use a right triangle for an internal common tangent of equal circles.

lessons.title: Turn proportion into a multiplier
knowledge: Turn percentage changes into successive multipliers and divide by their product to recover an original amount.
Write direct or inverse proportionality using a fixed constant.
Translate ratios into fractions of a whole and use the correct length, area or volume scale.
Distinguish simple interest, compound growth and the order of deposits or withdrawals.

lessons.title: Read tables and histograms
knowledge: Recover histogram frequencies from bar widths multiplied by density.
Estimate grouped means using midpoints and distinguish grouped estimates from exact summaries.
Find mean, median, mode and range from frequency data.
Select and construct suitable bar, pie, pictogram, two-way, discrete-line, time-series or cumulative displays.

lessons.title: Estimate an integral with trapezia
knowledge: Use n+1 heights for n trapezium strips and double only the interior heights.
Compute unequal-width trapezia individually.
Determine over- or underestimation from chord position relative to the curve, rather than increasing/decreasing behaviour.
Track signed approximation error through scaling and constants; recognise an exact semicircle integral geometrically.

lessons.title: Read the domain, then AND, OR and NOT
knowledge: Fix the allowed inputs before deciding whether a statement is true.
AND requires both statements; inclusive OR permits either or both; NOT reverses the truth of the whole statement.
Negating a strict inequality includes its equality boundary.
Count whole true statements at the same input when exactly two or exactly one are required.
Some means at least one; not prime is not equivalent to composite because 1 is neither.

lessons.title: Translate IF and ONLY IF before reasoning
knowledge: Identify the premise and conclusion by rewriting a sentence as an if-then implication.
A if B means B implies A; A only if B means A implies B.
If and only if requires both implication directions.
An implication fails precisely when its premise is true and its conclusion false; a false premise is not a counterexample.
A restriction on selected objects need not require any objects to be selected.

lessons.title: Reverse and negate for the contrapositive
knowledge: The converse reverses an implication and needs its own justification.
The contrapositive reverses and negates both clauses and is equivalent to the original implication.
A true premise forces its conclusion, and a false conclusion forces a false premise.
Knowing the conclusion alone does not establish the premise; denying the premise does not deny the conclusion.
Chains of implications can rule out statements as the sole true statement.

lessons.title: Test NECESSARY and SUFFICIENT separately
knowledge: Keep the target fixed: sufficiency tests condition implies target, while necessity tests target implies condition.
Classify a condition by proving each successful direction and giving an allowed counterexample for each failed direction.
Necessary and sufficient describes both directions, as in an if-and-only-if condition.
A stronger condition may be sufficient without being necessary.
For ax+by=c with nonzero coefficients, gradient and intercept signs are determined by -a/b and c/b.

lessons.title: Who is chosen first: EVERY or SOME?
knowledge: Every quantifies over all allowed inputs; there exists requires at least one allowed witness.
Read nested choices in order: a later witness may depend on an earlier input.
One fixed witness working for all inputs is a stronger requirement than choosing a witness separately for each input.
Construct a witness to prove existence and choose a defeating input to disprove a proposed fixed universal witness.
The same existence statement may change truth when its domain changes from integers to reals.

lessons.title: Negate the whole claim, keeping the domain
knowledge: Negate from the outer quantifier inward, swapping every and there exists without changing their order or domains.
The failure of a universal statement is one allowed counterexample; the failure of existence means all allowed candidates fail.
Negating AND gives an OR of negations, while negating OR gives an AND of negations.
To negate an implication, require its premise and the negation of its conclusion.
An if-and-only-if statement fails when exactly one of its two conditions is true; preserve equality when negating inequalities.

lessons.title: Disprove a claim with one allowed example
knowledge: A counterexample must satisfy every hypothesis and violate the conclusion.
For an implication, a true premise and false conclusion are both required.
One counterexample disproves an always-claim, while many successful cases do not prove it.
Check divisibility and primality against their definitions when choosing an integer counterexample.
Negative real inputs can defeat claims that squaring preserves order.

lessons.title: Turn definitions into a direct proof
knowledge: Represent arbitrary even integers as 2k and arbitrary odd integers as 2k+1, with integer k.
Use separate variables for independently chosen integers.
A direct proof begins with the assumptions and uses justified algebra to expose the required form.
To prove divisibility, express the result as the divisor times an integer.
Algebraic representations cover all permitted inputs; numerical tests alone do not.

lessons.title: Cover every case
knowledge: Choose cases that exhaust the stated domain and prove the claim in every case.
Even and odd cases include all integers, including zero and negative integers.
Use |x|=x for x>=0 and |x|=-x for x<0; assign boundary points to a case.
Integer squares leave remainder 0 or 1 modulo 4, as shown by parity cases.
For sums of absolute values, split at each point where an inner expression changes sign.

lessons.title: Assume the opposite and find an impossibility
knowledge: A contradiction proof assumes the denial of the desired conclusion and identifies a precise incompatible fact.
Rationals are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, and division by a nonzero rational.
Use rational closure to prove a rational plus an irrational, or a nonzero rational times an irrational, is irrational.
The impossibility of a negative real square can finish an inequality contradiction.
Showing a numerator and denominator share a factor contradicts rational representation only when lowest terms was assumed.

lessons.title: Find the first unsupported step
knowledge: Check each inference using only the assumptions and earlier justified lines, and stop at the first unsupported step.
A true conclusion does not make an invalid or incomplete proof correct.
Circular reasoning assumes the conclusion that the proof is meant to establish.
Dividing by an expression that may vanish can lose a solution; rearrangement and factorisation retain that case.
Squaring is valid forwards, but its candidate roots must be checked in the original equation.

lessons.title: Check what division loses and squaring adds
knowledge: Before cancelling an expression, check and handle the case where it equals zero.
Rearranging to a zero product can preserve solutions that division would discard.
Squaring an equality gives a necessary condition, but the squared equation may contain additional candidate roots.
Substitute candidates back into the original equation, respecting the nonnegative square root.
Equal function outputs need not imply equal inputs, as with squares and supplementary sine values.

lessons.title: Track signs before using an algebraic rule
knowledge: Multiplication or division by a negative number reverses an inequality.
An unknown multiplier sign may require positive, negative and zero cases.
For c>0, |z|>=c means z<=-c or z>=c, including both equality endpoints.
The zero-product rule requires a product equal to zero; a nonzero product does not fix individual factors.
Use the stated signs to bound ratios of negative numbers.

lessons.title: Separate height, gradient and signed area
knowledge: Function value, derivative and integral represent different quantities and must be tested separately.
Adding a constant changes height without changing the derivative.
A zero derivative gives a horizontal tangent and need not give a maximum or minimum.
Check behaviour on both sides before classifying a stationary point.
A zero signed integral can result from cancellation and does not force zero geometric area or a zero function.

lessons.title: Test both directions with allowed examples
knowledge: Test sufficiency and necessity as separate implications, using allowed counterexamples for directions that fail.
A sorted odd-length list has a middle entry; an even-length median averages the middle two entries.
Repetitions may make an even-length median an entry, while distinctness changes that conclusion.
Do not add assumptions such as positive, distinct or nonzero unless stated.
Apply the direction tests to divisibility, equations, inequalities and logarithmic conditions.

lessons.title: Check the argument, not just the conclusion
knowledge: Locate the first inference not supported by earlier proof lines.
A true one-way implication does not establish its converse; even a true converse needs justification.
A polynomial having no real linear factors does not imply that its integer values are prime.
Squaring gives candidates that require substitution into the original equation.
Cancellation requires a nonzero factor; rational closure can supply the contradiction in irrationality proofs.

lessons.title: Collect all contributions to a coefficient
knowledge: To find a coefficient in a product, list every pair of exponents whose sum is the target exponent.
Multiply the matching coefficients and add all contributions.
The coefficient of x^k in (1+x)^n is the binomial coefficient n choose k.
Substituting x=1 sums all coefficients; it gives one target coefficient only when the contributing terms exhaust that whole row.
For a constant term with positive and negative powers, require the total exponent to be zero.

lessons.title: Use the interval before comparing values
knowledge: Establish an ordering throughout the allowed interval before applying an outer function.
On 0<x<1, x^2<x<sqrt(x).
An exponential base greater than 1 preserves exponent order, while a base between 0 and 1 reverses it.
For continuous functions on [a,b] with a<b, strict pointwise ordering throughout (a,b) gives the same strict ordering of their integrals from a to b.
Read |x-a| as distance from a; midpoint boundaries solve comparisons of distances and intersections of their solution intervals.

lessons.title: Use geometry to test a universal claim
knowledge: Translate a geometric condition into lengths, areas or angles before deciding what it forces.
Triangle area with two sides and the included angle is half the product of the sides and the sine of that angle.
For angles strictly between 0 and 180 degrees, equal sine allows equal or supplementary angles.
A nonsquare rectangle inscribed in a circle gives equal centre-to-side triangle areas without regularity.
A symmetric example proves possibility, while a universal symmetry claim needs proof or an allowed irregular counterexample.

lessons.title: Complete each stage of a proof
knowledge: Existence needs an allowed solution; uniqueness needs proof that every solution equals that candidate.
A necessary candidate condition must be completed by substitution in the original problem or by reversible steps.
A contradiction proof retains the original assumptions, denies the target and finishes with explicitly incompatible facts.
Order definitions and conditions before proof lines that use them.
Rewrite logarithm definitions as powers and regroup exponents to connect a longer chain without assuming its conclusion.
Equal products do not force equality of corresponding factors.

lessons.title: Integer cases and supplied definitions
knowledge: Cover every possible remainder modulo a positive integer to prove a divisibility or remainder claim.
A prime divisible by another prime must equal that prime, so check the prime itself before declaring a multiple composite.
Products of consecutive integers provide small factors; divisibility by 2 and 3 ensures divisibility by 6, but overlapping factors cannot be counted twice.
For a supplied definition, preserve the order of member, factor and partner choices, allowing later choices to depend on earlier ones.
Negating every member has a suitable choice means one member has no suitable choice.
Keep other-member restrictions explicit: self-divisibility cannot supply a different partner.

lessons.title: Use an identity at useful inputs
knowledge: An identity holds at every allowed input; useful substitutions can make function arguments coincide or produce simultaneous equations.
Opposite heights equally spaced around a centre imply a zero value at that centre and signed integral cancellation on intervals with that midpoint.
Symmetry about one centre does not guarantee cancellation on an interval with a different midpoint.
Write the transformed input for each graph operation, then compare the two operation orders.
An identity f(x+T)=f(x) establishes a period, not necessarily the smallest positive period; positive integer multiples are also periods.
Replacing x by -x reflects roots and exchanges their positive and negative signs.

lessons.title: Find the full parameter range
knowledge: Check parameter values at which an equation changes degree before using a quadratic discriminant or dividing by a coefficient.
A nondegenerate quadratic has two distinct real roots for positive discriminant and one distinct repeated root for zero discriminant.
The substitution u=x^2 retains u>=0: positive u gives two real x values, zero gives one and negative u gives none.
Two distinct positive roots of the quadratic in u are needed for four distinct real roots of an even quartic; use discriminant, root sum and product.
Use cubic turning heights to classify real-root counts and inspect zero turning heights at parameter boundaries.
Prove the full necessary-and-sufficient range; a narrower sufficient condition alone does not describe all successful parameters.

lessons.title: Test claims about whole functions
knowledge: A functional counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis everywhere on the required domain or interval.
Increasing function height does not imply increasing gradient, and positive height does not imply positive gradient.
An integral of a square is nonnegative, while an ordinary signed integral may cancel.

On a nonempty forward interval, subtract shared integration intervals to isolate a sign constraint; for a continuous function, a nonpositive integral forces at least one nonpositive value, not nonpositivity everywhere.
The distinct roots of a product are the combined roots of its factors, with overlaps counted once.
A nonzero cubic has opposite-sign tails and cannot be positive on the entire real line.

additionalConcepts.title: Calculate with signed numbers and fractions
knowledge: Place value determines a digit’s contribution; compare signed numbers on a number line, where the number further right is larger.
Subtracting a negative adds its positive value; multiplication or division of two numbers with the same sign is positive, and with different signs is negative.
Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions, use a common denominator when adding or subtracting, and divide by a nonzero fraction by multiplying by its reciprocal.
Work through brackets, then powers and roots, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right.
A reciprocal is \(1/a\) for \(a\ne0\); squaring and cubing mean repeated multiplication, while cube roots reverse cubing, so \(\sqrt[3]{-8}=-2\).

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · M2.1, M2.2, M2.4, M2.6, M2.10

example.question: Evaluate \((-1\tfrac12+\tfrac34)\div(-\tfrac38)\).
steps: Convert the mixed number: \(-1\tfrac12=-\tfrac32=-\tfrac64\).
Calculate the bracket: \(-\tfrac64+\tfrac34=-\tfrac34\).
Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal: \(-\tfrac34\times(-\tfrac83)=2\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A minus sign before a mixed number applies to the whole number: \(-1\tfrac12=-\tfrac32\), not \(-\tfrac12\).

additionalConcepts.title: Use prime factors to find HCF and LCM
knowledge: A prime is an integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive factors; 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Every integer greater than 1 has a unique product of prime factors, apart from their order; repeated factors can be written as powers.
A factor divides a number exactly, and a multiple is an integer times that number; divisibility can be checked by comparing prime-factor exponents.
The highest common factor uses the smallest exponent of each shared prime, while the lowest common multiple uses the largest exponent of every prime present.
For positive integers \(a,b\), \(\operatorname{HCF}(a,b)\operatorname{LCM}(a,b)=ab\).

example.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 120.
steps: Factorise: \(72=2^3\times3^2\) and \(120=2^3\times3\times5\).
Take shared minimum powers: \(\operatorname{HCF}=2^3\times3=24\).
Take all maximum powers: \(\operatorname{LCM}=2^3\times3^2\times5=360\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A common multiple must contain enough copies of every required prime; being divisible by each distinct prime once is not sufficient.

additionalConcepts.title: Recognise exponential and logarithmic graphs
knowledge: For \(a>0\), the graph of \(y=a^x\) has positive outputs and passes through \((0,1)\) and \((1,a)\).
For \(a>1\) the exponential increases, while for \(0<a<1\) it decreases; in each case \(y=0\) is a horizontal asymptote, whereas \(a=1\) gives the constant graph \(y=1\).
For \(a>0\) and \(a\ne1\), \(y=\log_a x\) has domain \(x>0\), passes through \((1,0)\) and \((a,1)\), and has vertical asymptote \(x=0\).
A logarithm increases for \(a>1\) and decreases for \(0<a<1\), so applying a decreasing logarithm reverses an inequality.
The graphs of \(y=a^x\) and \(y=\log_a x\) are reflections in \(y=x\) because their inputs and outputs are interchanged.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · MM5.1, MM5.2, MM8.1, M4.12

example.question: Which standard exponential or logarithmic graph has domain \(x>0\), decreases, passes through \((1,0)\) and \((\tfrac12,1)\), and has vertical asymptote \(x=0\)?
steps: The domain and vertical asymptote match a logarithm, rather than an exponential.
For \(y=\log_a x\), the point \((a,1)\) identifies the base, giving \(a=\tfrac12\).
The base lies between 0 and 1, consistent with the graph decreasing.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A positive exponential base does not always give an increasing graph; bases between 0 and 1 reverse the direction.

additionalConcepts.title: Name geometric objects and recognise symmetry
knowledge: A point records a location, a line extends in both directions, a line segment has two endpoints, and a plane is a flat surface extending in all directions.
A vertex is a corner; an edge is where faces of a solid meet, while the sides of a polygon are line segments.
Parallel lines in a plane never meet; perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, and the middle letter of \(\angle ABC\) names its vertex \(B\).
The angle subtended by segment \(AB\) at \(C\) is \(\angle ACB\); a polygon is a closed plane figure with straight sides, and a regular polygon has equal sides and equal interior angles.

A line of symmetry reflects a shape onto itself; rotational symmetry of order \(k\) gives \(k\) matching positions in one full turn, and a regular \(n\)-gon has \(n\) symmetry lines and rotational order \(n\).

example.question: A regular hexagon is rotated about its centre: what is the smallest positive angle that makes it coincide with itself, and how many lines of symmetry does it have?
steps: Its six equally spaced vertices divide a full turn into six equal turns.
The smallest turn is \(360^\circ/6=60^\circ\).
Three symmetry lines join opposite vertices and three join midpoints of opposite sides.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Equal side lengths alone do not make a polygon regular: its interior angles must also be equal.

additionalConcepts.title: Use angle facts, parallel lines and polygon sums
knowledge: Angles around a point total \(360^\circ\), angles on a straight line total \(180^\circ\), and perpendicular lines form \(90^\circ\) angles.
Vertically opposite angles at the intersection of two straight lines are equal.
When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles and alternate angles are equal, while co-interior angles total \(180^\circ\).
A triangle has interior-angle sum \(180^\circ\), a quadrilateral has sum \(360^\circ\), and a triangle’s exterior angle equals the sum of its two opposite interior angles.

A simple \(n\)-sided polygon has interior-angle sum \((n-2)180^\circ\); the exterior turning angles of a convex polygon total \(360^\circ\), so a regular polygon has exterior angle \(360^\circ/n\) and interior angle \(180^\circ-360^\circ/n\).

example.question: A regular polygon has interior angle \(150^\circ\); how many sides does it have?
steps: An interior angle and its adjacent exterior angle lie on a straight line, so the exterior angle is \(180^\circ-150^\circ=30^\circ\).
The exterior angles total \(360^\circ\), and all are equal because the polygon is regular.
The number of sides is \(360/30=12\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Equal corresponding or alternate angles require parallel lines; a diagram that merely looks parallel is not enough.

additionalConcepts.title: Use the defining properties of triangles and quadrilaterals
knowledge: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three \(60^\circ\) angles, an isosceles triangle has two equal sides with equal opposite angles, and a scalene triangle has no equal sides; acute, right-angled and obtuse describe its angles.
A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal, opposite angles equal, adjacent angles supplementary, and diagonals that bisect each other.

A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles and equal diagonals; a rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides, perpendicular diagonals and diagonals that bisect its angles; a square has both sets of properties.
A trapezium has a pair of parallel opposite sides; an isosceles trapezium has equal nonparallel sides and equal base angles, but a general trapezium need not have those extra properties.

A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides, and the diagonal joining the vertices where those equal pairs meet is a symmetry line that perpendicularly bisects the other diagonal; derive needed side and angle facts by drawing a diagonal and using triangles.

example.question: In parallelogram \(ABCD\), the vertices are in order and \(\angle DAB=68^\circ\); find the other three interior angles.
steps: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so \(\angle BCD=68^\circ\).
Adjacent angles are supplementary because opposite sides are parallel, so \(\angle ABC=180^\circ-68^\circ=112^\circ\).
The remaining opposite pair gives \(\angle CDA=112^\circ\); the four angles total \(360^\circ\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A rhombus need not have right angles, and a rectangle need not have four equal sides; perpendicular diagonals alone do not force a square.

additionalConcepts.title: Label the sides before using right-triangle ratios
knowledge: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; opposite and adjacent are named relative to the chosen acute angle \(\theta\), with adjacent excluding the hypotenuse.
The ratios are \(\sin\theta=\text{opposite}/\text{hypotenuse}\), \(\cos\theta=\text{adjacent}/\text{hypotenuse}\), and \(\tan\theta=\text{opposite}/\text{adjacent}\).
Pythagoras gives \(a^2+b^2=c^2\) when \(c\) is the hypotenuse; rearrange a ratio to find a length or identify an angle from its known exact ratio.
For a general triangle, a perpendicular height can create right triangles; in three dimensions, select the correct face, cross-section or projection before applying the same rules.

example.question: A right-angled triangle has sides of length \(6\), \(8\) and \(10\), with \(\theta\) opposite the side of length \(6\); find \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\).
steps: The hypotenuse is \(10\), and \(6^2+8^2=10^2\) confirms the right triangle.
Relative to \(\theta\), the opposite side is \(6\) and the adjacent side is \(8\).
Therefore \(\sin\theta=6/10\), \(\cos\theta=8/10\), and \(\tan\theta=6/8\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Opposite and adjacent swap when you change the chosen acute angle; the hypotenuse never changes.

additionalConcepts.title: Count polynomial roots from signs and degree
knowledge: A polynomial graph is continuous. If its values at two inputs have opposite signs, it must cross the horizontal axis at least once between them.
Values of the same sign do not rule out roots between them: the graph may cross twice or touch the axis. Check separately whether an endpoint itself is a root.
A nonzero polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) distinct real roots. A repeated root counts only once when the question asks for distinct roots.
For sufficiently large positive or negative inputs, the leading term determines the sign. Use its coefficient and whether its degree is odd or even to establish the two tails.
Find disjoint intervals that each contain a root, then compare this lower bound with the degree's upper bound. When these bounds agree, the root count is exact.

example.question: Show that \(f(x)=x^3-4x\) has exactly three distinct real roots by considering signs and degree.
steps: There is a sign change on each of \((-3,-1)\), \((-1,1)\) and \((1,3)\). Continuity gives at least one root in each of these disjoint intervals, so at least three distinct roots.
The polynomial is a nonzero cubic, so it has at most three distinct real roots. Therefore it has exactly three.
As a check, \(x^3-4x=x(x-2)(x+2)\), giving the three roots \(-2,0,2\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A sign change proves at least one root, not exactly one. Do not conclude there are no roots between two values of the same sign.

additionalConcepts.title: Connect changing gradient, curvature and chords
knowledge: The second derivative is the derivative of the gradient. If \(f\prime\prime>0\) throughout an interval, the gradient increases and the curve bends upwards; if \(f\prime\prime<0\), the gradient decreases and the curve bends downwards.
On an upward-bending interval, a chord joining two points lies above the intervening curve; on a downward-bending interval it lies below. This explains the sign of trapezium-rule error.
For a polynomial with \(f\prime\prime\ge0\) throughout an interval, chord and curve may coincide where the graph is linear. A non-strict midpoint inequality permits equality.
The sign of the function height or its first derivative does not determine curvature. Vertical translations change neither the first nor the second derivative.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · MM6.1(b), MM6.3 and MM7.5
TMUA 2018 · Paper 2 · Question 18, worked answer pages 21–22

example.question: For \(f(x)=x^2+3\) on \([-1,1]\), compare the one-strip trapezium estimate with the exact integral. Does the changing sign of the gradient alter the conclusion?
steps: The gradient is \(2x\) and the second derivative is \(2\). The gradient changes sign at zero, but it increases throughout the interval.
Both endpoint heights are \(4\), so the chord is the horizontal line at height \(4\), above the curve except at the endpoints. The trapezium estimate is \(2\times4=8\).
The exact integral is \([x^3/3+3x]_{-1}^{1}=20/3\), less than \(8\).
example.answer: The trapezium estimate is an overestimate by \(4/3\); the sign of the gradient is not what determines this.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Do not confuse an increasing function with an increasing gradient. A single observed trapezium overestimate does not prove one curvature sign everywhere.
